title: SCALPELLO-GDP: a frontier model edits the weights of Qwen3.5-0.8B directly. One Householder reflection of a 'repetitive re-checking' direction lifts held-out math accuracy from 9.4% to 53.6% (384 paired problems), with no training

headline_result.text: A Householder reflection of 12 attention output projections along an Astra-chosen 'repetitive re-checking' direction raised accuracy on 384 held-out practice problems from 9.38% to 53.65% at an 8,192-token cap, while a random-direction reflection gave +3.1 points on the development set.
headline_result.quote: accuracy 9.38% → 53.65% (+44.27 ± 2.56 points, 95% bootstrap CI [39.32; 49.22]; exact McNemar p = 5.8 × 10−50 ); answers cut at the token limit 91.7% → 28.1%.

key_claims.claim: The edit is a closed-form rank-one Householder reflection computed from a difference of means over three editor-written text pairs; no gradients were used.
key_claims.quote: A training-free, closed-form, rank-one edit of 12 weight matrices: a Householder reflection of their output along one unit vector u.

key_claims.claim: A reflection of the same matrices along a random direction had little effect on the 32 development problems.
key_claims.quote: A norm-preserving reflection of the same matrices is therefore not enough by itself; the direction matters.

key_claims.claim: Almost all gains were problems where the original model ran out of tokens; the edit adds no mathematical knowledge.
key_claims.quote: Of the 171 gains, 170 were answers in which the original model reached the 8,192-token limit without writing any boxed answer; only 1 was a completed but wrong original answer.

key_claims.claim: Because the gain is about finishing, it would likely shrink with the original 32,768-token budget.
key_claims.quote: Because the improvement consists of finishing, it says nothing about new mathematical ability, and part of it would shrink with a longer token budget (Section 9).

key_claims.claim: The replication used half the forward budget and a quarter of the generation length of the MIT setup, at an editor API cost of $8.43.
key_claims.quote: Editor cost: $8.43 for 92 calls (cap $60); GPU work was local.

key_claims.claim: The edit was frozen before held-out evaluation.
key_claims.quote: “Fix candidate B2 attention-only for independent validation. No edits will be selected using held-out results.”

limitations_stated.text: Held-out cohorts come from training splits; MATH-500 and GSM8K test were not run.
limitations_stated.quote: Held-out cohorts come from the GSM8K and MATH train- ing splits (decontaminated practice files); MATH-500 and the GSM8K test set were not run.

limitations_stated.text: Shorter 8,192-token budget inflates the gain from finishing in time.
limitations_stated.quote: 8,192 generated tokens instead of 32,768; part of the gain is “finishing in time”, and with a longer budget the original model would finish more often, so the gain is likely smaller.

limitations_stated.text: One sample per problem, one run, one editor; development used only 32 problems.
limitations_stated.quote: One sample per problem, one run, one editor, fp16 on a T4; development used only 32 problems.

notes_for_review: An independent low-budget replication of the MIT Qwen3.5-0.8B loop-repair experiment with GPT-6 Astra as editor; the resulting edit is essentially a mechanical diff-of-means direction plus Householder reflection, the kind of edit a human could compute without an LLM. It includes a random-direction control and clean held-out cohorts, but uses an 8,192-token cap (which makes the base model look worse), practice-split problems rather than MATH-500, one run, no gradient or prompt/decoding baselines. The author explicitly attributes the gain to stopping loops, not new ability, and the edited weights and code are released; bilingual IT/EN document, quotes taken from the English half.
